 Expect something new weekly.

articles.title: The Gold Mine
articles.subtitle: Keep mining away, you’re bound to find something.
articles.description: Keep mining away, you’re bound to find something.
articles.content:
Last week, I imagined having a gold mine.

Everyday, I would have the opportunity to mine some gold. However, I don’t know how to go down and mine myself. Lucky for me, I have workers who are willing to go and search for gold for me.

Early on, my miners find no gold. They go down and return with nothing, over and over until I grow impatient. This is a barren mine, I think. And so I stop sending them down.

Life goes on, void of gold. One day, I remember the mine. I wonder if maybe there is some gold in it, and that maybe I simply didn’t give my miners enough time to search for it.

I return to the mine, and this time I wait a long time. My workers come back one-by-one, each as empty handed as the last. My eyes fall lower with each successive failure.

As I’m about to give up for the final time, to resign myself to the belief that my gold mine has no gold, a worker comes out. Their hands reach out, full of gray dust. In the dust, a sparkle of light unlike anything that has come from the mine. Native gold.

It’s not much, not worth enough to rationalize the time so far spent by my miners and me, but what the meaning is priceless. There is gold in this mine.

I begin regularly visiting the mine. Sending miners down and reacting as one-by-one they come back empty handed with a glum expression, or with some bit of raw gold, ready to be processed and released to the world. I yearn to go into the mines myself, to understand what it is that happens beneath the surface, but the only thing I seem capable of is taking their nuggets and gold dust and polishing it into something others will see as valuable.

From my perspective, it’s like magic that they can arise from the earth with gold for me.

Despite not understanding exactly what they do in the mine, I begin to learn more about my gold mine. I notice that although gold is rare, there are ways to increase the likelihood of finding it.

  1. Giving my miners time to mine. They need lots of time to look for gold.

  2. Treating my miners well. How rested they are, their access to nutrition, the level of respect they feel, all plays into their gold output.

  3. Believing in the mine’s reserves. There are periods of high output when veins are found, and stretches of lack in between. Those times between are the most important for me to continue sending miners down. The mine is never truly exhausted.

So, this obviously isn’t about mining in real life. It may be an obvious analogy (or maybe not, I honestly have no idea), but I think this is a pretty good one for creativity.

Creativity is typically spoken about as something frozen in place–this person is creative and has always and will always be this way, this other person is less so and will always be that way, but I think this analogy gives us a better understanding of how creativity truly works in individuals.

We all have access to a mine and we all have our own group of miners1. Mining requires being in a mental space in which our miners are able to mine–it could be writing, poking around on a piano keyboard, or ideating on a problem while walking. Our miners have a certain level of skill and familiarity (or lack thereof) around certain areas within the mine, and that goes hand-in-hand with the mistaken beliefs many of us carry about our own gold mines.

For example, someone who is reinforced as a prodigal painter will spend much more time exploring that part of the mine, with lots of belief that something will be returned. Their miners will get increasingly better at mining that specific area, and it will result in someone who is very creative. We imagine that this is just how they are, without recognizing the amount of time that their miners have spent searching in this specific place.

On the other hand, someone who hasn’t been reinforced in this same way will likely see themselves as less creative (and it will be true). The mistaken belief, however, is that they are this way permanently–a belief that fulfills itself by keeping them from giving their miners any chance to learn.

1

In my analogy, the mine is the ideation space of all of our potential creations. The miners represent your subconscious thought processes (you can send them off to go explore, but you lose access until they return). You can fill in the rest of the analogy.

articles.title: Rapid Reinforcement Loops
articles.subtitle: The unsung power of immediate gratification
articles.description: The unsung power of immediate gratification
articles.content:
This will be my 3rd week straight writing about stand-up comedy. I will explain without apologizing–it’s been an extremely intense and novel experience with so many lessons in the very short span that I’ve been doing it (as I write this, I have summed up a total of 45 minutes on stage).

​Today, I want to talk about the motivational power of rapid reinforcement loops. As I explain what I mean, I want to challenge you to consider whether there are projects of your own to which this could apply. I, in return, will do the same in other areas of my life, outside this new hobby.

​Brand new comedians rarely get “good” stage time. I watched the movie “Is This Thing On” earlier this year, which tells the story of a man going through a personality crisis after splitting with his wife, and finding stand-up comedy in the midst of it.

Here’s my qualm. The first time he tries it, he is told that if he puts his name on the list, his cover will be, well, covered (and this is the whole reason he does it). He then performs to a packed room of people all fiercely interested in his comedy.

Unfortunately, this isn’t quite how it works (and for good reason).

Let’s walk through it logically. People go to shows because they think there is a strong likelihood of being entertained. Open mics are an extreme toss-up. Anybody who can write their own name can sign up. Funny moments, while they still exist, become fewer and farther between.

Unlike the movie, open mic nights often end up being a half-filled room of other open-mic’ers. If you’re lucky, there are a few people who have come for their own enjoyment.

That brings us to rapid-reinforcement loops.​

Rapid-reinforcement loops happen when work (or lack thereof) is rewarded or punished very quickly after it happened.

For this example–if I write a good joke one day, the loop is extremely tight, because it is likely that night that I will be rewarded for it.

There is also a much stronger negative-reinforcement loop associated with not doing the work, because of the open-mic audience dilemma discussed above: the audience has likely seen the old stuff before, because they’re the same open-mic’ers trying to get on stage themselves.. If I don’t write new jokes, a “good” joke that’s been used already won’t work because the bulk of the people watching have heard it before.

This is an intense pressure, but when social acceptance and potential ostracization are on the line, it generates explosive motivation. If I do write, I am rewarded. If I don’t, I am punished. Both things happen rapidly and forcefully.

This reinforcement loop is in direct contrast to other projects I’ve worked on over the years, like the newsletter you’re reading right now.

Occasionally I will receive feedback, but it’s often delayed and infrequent. The motivation is completely self-driven, for the simple reason that I don’t want to break my 150+ week streak. That’s also a strong motivator (who would want to break a chain like that), but that doesn’t help anybody if you don’t already have a chain going. Stand up is the complete opposite; I don’t write to maintain a streak, I write because I see the immediate impact of writing.​

So with that, I’ll challenge you to seek out reinforcement loops in your life and work. If you struggle with motivation, it could easily be because your actions are not being rewarded (or punished) rapidly. If you want to get in shape, start with something that you can see immediate improvement in, like a 1 mile time trial or lifting weights (incremental progress can be very motivating). If it’s a creative project, push yourself to seek feedback from others at every stage.

I talk about something related called behavioral momentum in this week’s podcast episode, check it out: Get addicted to following your dreams | Willpower Podcast #115

Leave a comment if you come up with a reinforcement loop specific to your pursuit and would like to commit to it!

articles.title: Fear Crossing Over
articles.subtitle: You don't have to fight forever. Just until it stops feeling like a fight.
articles.description: You don't have to fight forever. Just until it stops feeling like a fight.
articles.content:
Last week, I talked about the initial friction of starting stand-up comedy: specifically the anxious physiological response that would set in when thinking about doing it. That was one of the “types” of hard, the one based in fear, not boredom.

Today, I want to offer a nugget of hope on that same subject, after another week of life experience.

On Monday, I went to another open mic. The first since the “return” from last week–my first mic in 9 months. I noticed that I was slightly calmer this week, though I still noticed my heart rate increasing throughout the day alongside a few “fuck this” ledges that I had to talk myself down from.

Then came an interesting moment on stage. I told a joke that got a mild response from the homogenous crowd of comedians. And for just a second, something clicked inside. Not on a cognitive level (though I could make up some rationalization for it), but on some deeper emotional level.

I walked back to the car after that, with a feeling I had never had before. I had a genuine desire to do it again.

There are going to be hard things on the path to the life you want. Both of the “types of hard” I defined last week will show up. However, there are sometimes where it simply isn’t hard. Where natural excitement and desire lines up perfectly with the thing you are trying to achieve, and suddenly feels fun and exciting.

At the same time, I can’t claim to now have no fear of doing standup. Yesterday, I went to 2 new mics, and each time I went up I felt the familiar anxious energy. The difference this time is that a certain calculation had flipped.

Whenever we are weighing whether to do a hard action of the fearful type, our brain makes an unconscious calculation. Simply stated, it measures the fear of doing it and compares that to the expected reward of doing the action.

If the fear surpasses the expected reward, I will not feel motivated to do the thing. That’s where I will feel either

  1. Incapable of doing it.

  2. Apathetic and disinterested in the idea of doing it.

Whether it is a) or b) will depend on the way your body perceived the fear itself, which is a separate calculation

There is a point, though, at which the expected reward of the action crosses its associated fear. That was the moment I had onstage last week.

.

The specific trajectory of each line can change. You may have the exact same amount of fear, and the expected reward increases to meet it. Or, like in my case, the expected reward didn’t increase much, but my fear dropped substantially, falling beneath it. However it happens, our focus is on the crossover point, and more specifically, what comes after it.

What comes after this crossover point is almost magical (especially if you are used to fear dominating). Once those two lines cross, motivation becomes natural. No more need for tricks or mindset shifts, I begin to just want the thing. This is where “addiction” level obsessions set in.

For example, maybe you started going to the gym. One day, while you’re close to giving up out of embarrassment, you see that your weight has dropped 15 pounds over the month. Assuming that was your goal, your expected reward of working out skyrockets. The fear of embarrassment is still there, but is completely dominated, and you feel the natural desire to get into the gym.

I’m going to step back to the stand-up example to really reinforce the idea of natural motivation. Before this crossover point I had some type of motivation, or I wouldn’t have done it at all. The difference, however, was that it was forced motivation. It was the type of motivation that relies on cognitive reasoning rather than emotional understanding. This type of motivation is necessary at times–that’s how you get through the first month in the gym before the results start setting in–but the difference is incredible. Especially in terms of enjoyability.

Think about something in the past that you were excited about. It could be a meal after a long day, a TV show, seeing a friend, or something completely different. Because you were excited, there was a natural motivation to do that thing, or take the steps to get to that thing. That’s what I’m talking about. Imagine feeling that excitement to do the exact thing that is right now in your way. The thing is fun, it’s exciting, it’s something you look forward to. You will even exert effort just to be able to do it. It’s fun.

From our graph, we see that this “magic zone” comes only after the lines cross. That, of course, means that they were flipped before, and that’s a hard place to be. Being in that stage is the reason I spent 9 months avoiding going on stage.

So there is my nugget of hope. You may be in the initial stage, and the idea of confronting this fear in the forceful way that you have been feels like an eternal struggle. It isn’t. The struggle, as real and challenging as it is, only lasts until those lines cross.

Thanks for reading! If you’d like more, you can check out this weeks podcast:

If you’re interested in building willpower, join my willpower board to track your habits alongside me: https://board.williammulvaney.com

articles.title: Types of Hard
articles.subtitle: The two sides of the willpower coin
articles.description: The two sides of the willpower coin
articles.content:
Nine months ago I tried my first ever stand-up comedy open mic. It went as expected: terribly. To be fair, it was a room full of other open-mic’ers and not a single soul who had come there just to enjoy the show. The barista / bartender seemed to be the only person even willing to enjoy a joke or two.

I ended up doing it a few more times that same week, at other locations. Surprisingly, they went better. Then, I got caught up with life (running an ultramarathon will do that). It would be nine months until I even considered trying it again.

This week, we’re talking about hard things. The simple act of getting on stage and telling bad jokes, for me, is really fucking hard. But as we’ll realize, there are different types of hard, with one throughline on how to best deal with them. This understanding will help us to stand tall in the face of that which is “hard” in this world.

Last week, I finally got fed up with 2 things:

  1. The wastefulness of coming up with new jokes over the last 9 months with absolutely nothing to do with them.

  2. The feeling of being defeated. I didn’t want to have this “boogeyman” that I couldn’t confront. The longer I waited around, the more the fear grew (my subconscious seemed to be making the assumption that more avoidance = scarier obstacle).

So I bit the bullet, and decided I would do it again. On Sunday, I put it on my Google calendar for the following day (a good tactic I’ve learned to stop my future self from downplaying something I’m avoiding).

On the day of, I was very nervous. I went for a hard run before to shake out some of that. Still nervous. I sat by the pool after my run, letting myself think about what I was going up against. Would it always be this way? Was there any escape from these dang nerves that I was so uncomfortable with?

I got back and started driving to the open mic, leaving the stereo off to give myself time to settle. The idea behind that was: “There’s a limited amount of total nervousness I can feel. If I feel it all right now, I’m less likely to feel it when it matters1.”

I finally brought myself to a place of (relative) peace with the idea, and I got in line at the comedy club. It seemed long, and I knew it was capped at 20. A part of me really wanted to leave. I held my ground and waited.

Sure enough, I was around 24th in line and didn’t get a spot. I internally feigned disappointment, but inside I was relieved. I went to another spot with someone I met, where we similarly missed sign-ups. This was great–I could tell myself I had tried, but just due to external circumstances couldn’t get up.

Tuesday came around, and I went back. I still had to fight the nerves that day, but not nearly as much. I got to the club earlier, got on the list, and after 90 minutes of waiting, I went up and spent 3 minutes on stage.

It was a triumph. I had broken the dry spell.

On Wednesday, I decided not to go to any mics but I did plan to go to a Jiu Jitsu class. It had been over a month since I’d been in. The entire day, that was the plan. I felt zero nervousness to do it.

Then, the time to get ready and go rolled around.

Still no nerves, but an intense lethargy swelled throughout my body. Did I really want to do this? I had already run and worked out today, wasn’t that enough? I also hadn’t slept well the night before! Why was I forcing this?

Getting myself to go was going to be hard, but it felt nothing like the “hard” I had faced the two days prior.

I went to Jiu Jitsu, and it went fine (I promised myself that I would get something good for dinner if I went). The interesting thing I noticed was how hard it was to get myself to go, and how much this “hardness” contrasted with the “hardness” of trying stand-up comedy.

When chasing success2, there seem to be two types of “hard”.

  1. Confronting the fear of the unknown.

  2. Repeating an action with expected discomfort.

These cleanly categorize the two “hard”’s I faced this week. One (stand-up comedy) involves facing a new beast, something I don’t know well enough to know what to expect. The other (going to BJJ) is a well-known action with well-defined expectations.

There is nothing specific to these two actions that puts them in those categories. A professional comedian who has never done BJJ would probably feel these in reverse: going to an open-mic may feel like a drag while going to BJJ feels scary and unknown.

Interestingly, it’s not just the perception of the event that changes. The friction, the bodily experience that makes it seem hard, itself changes. These physiological reactions are almost pure opposites.

The day of the open mic, I felt nerves tingling in my chest and stomach. I had racing thoughts. My heart was pounding.

When deciding whether to go to BJJ, I felt slow and lethargic. Just the thought of it made me want to sit on the couch and eat something.

The mechanism by which this happens is relatively important, at least for right now. What is important is understanding this friction as what it is: resistance from the body that does not (always) need to be listened to3. This is some unconscious part of me saying “Hey, I don’t want to do this”, in two different dialects.

Most “hard” things can be broken into these two categories. And surprisingly, the hardness of them is often overcoming the physiological response. The two traits we often associate with doing these hard things are bravery and discipline, respectively.

When we break it down like this, both desirable traits are solely determined by my ability to temper the two bodily experiences and stay the course. That’s a pretty generalizable skill, isn’t it?

1

This is just a made-up idea. Don’t fact check if this is scientifically accurate.

2

Success is very broadly defined here. For me, success in stand-up comedy (or Brazilian Jiu Jitsu, for that matter) has nothing to do with the typical monetary definition.

3

I take it back. It should be listened to. That doesn’t, however, mean that it should be followed. Take it for what it’s worth.

articles.title: The Planning Paradox
articles.subtitle: Why thinking ahead gets harder the more you succeed
articles.description: Why thinking ahead gets harder the more you succeed
articles.content:
The Paradox of Planning

Why thinking ahead gets harder the more you succeed

I crossed the finish line, and it was all finally over. 1100 miles of training and 100 miles of performing. I sacrificed my body, shown through the comments from friends “You look so much smaller!” and the multiple-month recovery process that came next.

The motivation for this entire journey? A single piece of paper.

The Fear of Starting

I’m currently signed up for the BMW Dallas Marathon in December of this year. It will be my first race since the aforementioned ultra I completed last December, which to some extent stifled my interest in long distance running. Regardless, I’m back, and in a timespan (a year) that will likely not seem like much in the overall arc of my life.

The interesting thing with my signing up, however, is that I still have not made a training plan. Last year, preparing for a race that was almost 4 times the distance, I remember feeling lots of excitement as I conversed back and forth with ChatGPT to formulate the perfect running plan (while trying to give as much grace for its inability to consistently calculate the correct number of weeks until the race). I printed out the plan, realizing how important this piece of paper now was to me, how this would be my north star for the next 4 months.

Oops, never mind. The last week of training in the table was a week early. I fixed it and fired off a fresh copy of my Declaration, and I was set. Locked and loaded for the next 4 months.

With this memory floating around in my consciousness while I registered myself, I naturally assumed the first steps of my marathon prep would be the same. Since that moment, I simply haven’t created a plan. I know I have to (and the sooner the better – I only have 4 months ahead of me), but for some reason there is something stopping me from wanting to.

The Fun of Making (future) Unrealized Plans

There is a well-known cliché about New Year’s resolutions. That they don’t work. By now, I will bet that the majority of us have been told not to make them, in some way or another.

Yet, for any of us who have made them, I will bet that the process was fun. You sat down, dreamed of what it would be like to accomplish the thing you’re resolving to change (better fitness, more money, better relationships). And what happened?

Wild guess: you didn’t accomplish it.

This isn’t an attack. I’ve done the same thing before, spending hours having fun working on goals in a way that did nothing for me moving along the path to the goal. Then, when it came to the thing, I didn’t do it (broadly speaking, it often looks like trying to do it for some time, then inevitably failing). The next year, I go through the same process, having all of the fun in the world building the plan, then much less fun following through.

Marathon training

How does this tie into my training then? If I remember what I wrote earlier correctly, I said that I had lots of fun creating the plan, and then I did follow through, and did treat that piece of paper as sacred. Why then, am I talking about unrealized plan making?

The connection I’m drawing is not in the lack of follow–through– it’s in our propensity to plan for things we don’t actually see ourselves doing.

It’s easy for me to make a plan to run a shit ton of miles when I haven’t done it before (at least not to the extent needed here). The miles that I am entering on the spreadsheet are imaginary, just numbers that are contributing to this awesome accomplishment that has all of my focus.

When I try to make a spreadsheet now, each number I enter in comes with a memory of waking up early, wanting nothing more than to rest my already sore legs with more sleep, only to spend the entire morning running (or worse yet, waiting till the evening and spending the entire day dreading it). The plan has real weight, because I remember the feelings that these actions entail.

The Effect on Planning of Following Through

In times when I am not accomplishing, I love planning. Planning, in my mind, becomes completely disconnected from real outcomes (and the inputs). It is a self-contained activity that is done for fun–and any belief otherwise is wishful thinking.

When the results become real, the activity of planning becomes less fun, because every imagined input comes with the weight of the reality of doing it. It’s not “inputs magically produce this output that I want”; it instead becomes “I can only accomplish this outcome by manually putting in these required (and difficult) actions.”

If planning begins to seem like a challenge, or something to be avoided, this is actually a good sign. That is your brain recognizing “This guy/girl is fucking serious this time. We’re not dreaming anymore.” Don’t despair when it happens, and allow it to be as it is. You will naturally end up planning less, and the things you do plan will take up more space, and the likelihood of each plan being followed through will skyrocket.

articles.title: Threats & Challenges
articles.subtitle: How stand-up comedy can shrink your telomeres
articles.description: How stand-up comedy can shrink your telomeres
articles.content:
I recently started a book on a topic I’ve heard more and more about over the past few years: telomeres.

The book is by far the most popular on the subject, and one of the authors is a lead researcher in the field. It’s been interesting to read, but less than groundbreaking on a personal front. Rather than showing some new way to live longer, the authors show that many common-sense health practices lead to longer health spans (the amount of time you are capable of living your life uninhibited by age-related health issues), with the mechanism—the shortening of telomeres—being the shiny object.

Basically, things like sleeping better, eating cleaner, avoiding smoking & alcohol, and moving around regularly all slow the shrinking of telomeres.

And one of the biggest factors? Stress.

One of the most stressful things I did in the last year was trying a stand-up comedy open mic. Did that experience increase or decrease the rate of my telomeres shortening?

The relationship between stress and telomere length is not quite as simple as more stress = shorter telomeres. In fact, it can work in either direction. What matters is actually the type of stress, which is defined by the way that you view the stressor.

​That’s right: your attitude towards the stressor affects whether it is going to have a positive or negative impact on your telomeres and overall health. Your mind is quite literally the deciding factor for how your body responds.

​My first open mic was terrifying. I remember spending the entire day leading up to it feeling nervous and scared. Every time I thought about the upcoming event, my inner dialogue went to: “How do I get out of this?”

​The authors break the types of stressors into two groups, though I don’t think that they invented the categorizations.

​The categories are threat and challenge.

Here’s how the classification works:

​You perceive a stressor.

  1. Your subconscious brain makes a quick calculation: Are my perceived resources greater or lesser than the required resources to confront this stressor?

  2. A physiological reaction takes place depending on the answer.

  3. Your rate of telomere shrinkage increases or decreases based on the reaction.

Here’s the key part: that physiological reaction is different depending on how the stressor is categorized.​

If it feels like I don’t have the resources necessary to confront the stressor, my blood vessels will constrict, my blood pressure will increase, and my cognitive processing speed will decrease. Cortisol is released into the bloodstream. This is a threat: my brain goes into survival mode. Peripheral resistance increases. Telomere shrinkage rate increases.

If it feels like I do have the resources necessary, I will have a completely different physiological response. Adrenaline is released into the bloodstream. More blood flow is directed to the brain. Peripheral resistance decreases. Telomere shrinkage rate decreases (assuming this doesn’t happen too frequently—chronic stress seems to always be bad no matter the type).

Effectively, my body is going into “flight” or “fight”, respectively. In flight mode, I need to be aware of everything going on around me, so my periphery expands. My cognitive processing is less important, because getting away is quite a simple calculation. Blood is drawn to the core to keep me alive. Fight mode, on the other hand, gives me a chance to directly confront the stressor. My brain is needed in full force, and my attention needs to be incredibly narrow–only on the challenge in front of me.

Clearly, I was in flight mode that first time trying stand-up. Everyone in the cafe was there to have fun, yet in my mind, that lady calling names was a huge threat. I was even seated near the door. I thought about just getting up and walking out. When they called me, they’d just move on when they realized it.

I struggled to focus on what I had prepared. My hand holding the piece of paper I had prepared as a contingency shook as I read off of it.

The night was a success, simply because I did it. And I knew I had done it, but reflecting back, my memory seemed to cut out the moment after walking up on stage. I barely remembered the experience.

And so I signed up to do it again. Here I was, at a new place – freaking the fuck out again. Wanting to get out. Watching over a hundred people file into this club where I’m up 4th for a thing I’ve tried once before, and don’t even really remember doing. Wanting to get out.

I got myself up there. And then something happened when I started talking. People laughed.

It was like I was fighting a heavyweight boxer, and for the first time ever I realized he was human, and could be defeated. I can actually do this, a voice deep in my psyche called out.

I’m not going to claim that that second attempt went perfectly, that I killed and went on to become a stand-up comedian. I did it once more after that, and haven’t since (though I plan to change that soon).

The real insight into this event was the shift that happened when the task of winning over a huge crowd turned from a threat, something I didn’t see as possible and therefore wanted to run from, to a challenge.

What are the things in your life that you’re perceiving as threats? Is it possible they might turn to challenges, if you gave yourself the chance to confront them? Please leave a comment or reply directly, I’d love to hear from you.

If you’d like to hear more from me, check out the podcast.

I have also created 2 apps based around building habits:

  1. Grooves (analytical and impact-based).

  2. Habit Empire (gamified and progress-based).

articles.title: Goldilocks Discipline
articles.subtitle: Why our personal systems keep breaking
articles.description: Why our personal systems keep breaking
articles.content:
During college, I developed a pretty intense gym workout. Well, I didn’t develop it–it was more like a virus that jumped from one of my good friends to me. It was still early in the pandemic, so we hadn’t learned social distancing yet.

This workout routine included six days of workouts every week that ranged from 1.5 to 3 hours. Every day ended with a grounded ab routine. And the most intense part about it was the rigidity. I had to do it. If I missed a day for any reason, I knew that my next rest day would be transformed into a raincheck day, in which I would take on this workout.

I put on a whole lot of muscle. My cardio was good (partially from starting to learn Brazilian Jiu Jitsu). Then came a week when I missed 2 days.

The system wasn’t built for this! My subconscious brain screamed at me. What are we going to do? This is all going to fall apart. I felt the routine like sand in my fingers, and the more I grasped at it, the faster it slipped away.

I was able to hold it for some time by devising a system in which I would keep track of my missed days. I fell into ‘debt’, owing 3, 4, then 5 workouts. If I wanted to get back to even, I’d have to work out every day for a month straight.

And I continued to slip until I got to 10 due workouts. That’s where it completely fell apart. Like a skyscraper without enough give, my system broke under too much stress. It didn’t have a way to rebound–every single stressor piled on cumulative damage to the system until it couldn’t take any more.

You may have experienced something like this before. A life change, a habit, a new routine, something where it feels like “missing” once will create an incurable rupture. That fear is motivating because of how bad you expect to feel when it inevitably breaks.

The fear is also demotivating. When you consider going all in on something new, you remember what it might feel like to quit down the path. Then, you quit early, thinking “maybe if I don’t invest too much into this, I won’t be quite as mean to myself when it doesn’t work out.”

The system was too rigid.

When my system broke, I went to the drawing board. Through a mix of logical thought and subconscious fear, I realized that I needed a bit more “sway” in a workout routine, or I would end up with a routine that not only broke easily but also put me in a constant state of vigilance that the break was coming.

I wanted a skyscraper that could face the storms of life without a worry in my mind that it would topple.

So I made it nice and flexible. New rule: I didn’t have to work out unless I felt like it, when it made sense with my day. If I was tired after work, I would just head home instead of making the normal trip to the gym where I would lift and stick around for a BJJ class. Maybe with a stop for Chipotle along the way.

I began waking up later. With my overly rigid routine, I had been up at 6 every morning for work. I thought this was unrelated to my workouts (because I rarely worked out in the morning). Things started slipping in all areas. A weekly night out became standard. I ate out more often.​

Pretty quickly (with the aid of a motivational podcast or two), I realized that I had overcorrected. There had been too much give in this new system, to the point where it had no structure that I could lean on.

This is the more common scenario, and one you have almost certainly experienced before. You have a general idea of what you want to happen (get in shape, advance in your career, etc.), and you even know the steps to make it happen. The system that holds you to those steps, however, isn’t strong enough to keep you going when life’s winds come full force.

So you end up doing nothing, and slowly but surely, the system (if you can call it that) begins to fall apart. The skyscraper that was barely standing in the first place was blown over because there wasn’t enough rigidity to hold it up.

You feel bad, like a failure. You should have been more motivated. It feels like it was your fault. That’s not the real reason.

This system was too flexible.

So that leaves us searching for Goldilocks Discipline, the “just right” middle ground between our overly rigid and overly flexible systems.

Rather than walk you through my exact routine, I want to break down the principles that I believe make for a Goldilocks System.

  1. Self-governing. Like a good republic, the system should be able to adapt itself. My gym routine right now isn’t the same as it was 6 months ago, but it still exists. It adapts with the weather of life, as if there were builders constantly making changes to my skyscraper.

  2. Properly motivated. The overly rigid system was motivated by not wanting to break the system. The flexible one was motivated when motivation was remembered. We want our actions to be regularly motivated by our deepest reason for having a system in the first place.

  3. Intentionally designed. We should be deciding what we want the system to do. It should not be there simply because it seems like it should be. In both cases, that ends up with broken and fallen skyscrapers. We should build it with thought and with care (and the fact that you’ve gotten this far shows some willingness to try).

Skyscrapers will break. Over and over. Then, one won’t. And lucky for us, we just need the one to stand, and stand as an example of what we have accomplished and what we can then do again and again.

I would love to hear from you. What is your version of Goldilocks discipline? Are you often “too rigid” or “too flexible”?

If you would like to hear more from me, feel free to check out my podcast:

Or try out either of my apps:

Grooves

Habit Empire

articles.title: Accepting My Limits
articles.subtitle: When I don't prioritize, I do
articles.description: When I don't prioritize, I do
articles.content:
I have about 4 different major (or so I think) business projects I am trying to keep moving forward. And the next 3 weeks are a blend of visiting family, vacation, and other travel shenanigans.

Out of the many things I want to get done every day, many simply will not. It isn’t feasible to get them all done. That leaves me with two options:

  1. Shake my fist at the sky. I could wish to have more time to be able to get it all done.

  2. Accept that I can’t do everything I want, and pick the stuff that I really want to do.

Prioritizing

Last night, I sat in bed thinking about this “problem”. What I came to realize is that this is a perfect microcosm of life–a scaled-down version. This month I have to prioritize heavily, something I don’t feel like I’ve had to do recently. Guess what? I have been.

There is a harsh truth of life that we will never be able to do all of the things we want to do. It’s just not in the cards. I can dream all I want; it won’t all happen. And every time I ignore this reality, I am making it worse.

In life, I either choose my priorities, or they will choose me. There is no other option.

Sometimes it takes scoping down work time to 1-2 hours per day to realize this. Having an 8-hour workday feels endless–like there’s no way I can’t get done what I need to. That’s silly when we look at this extreme. There is nothing inherently different in that longer day that makes prioritization less important: if I don’t accept my limitations and make a choice to kill certain paths, I just end up doing more of the wrong stuff.

Acceptance

The first step, then, as is the first step in nearly every path in this realm, is acceptance. To move forward, I need to accept the reality that I will need to choose between the many ideas and dreams I have and become very clear.

​This can be high-level: accepting what I can or can’t do this year, in 5 years, or 10 years. It can also be extremely low-level: accepting that spending more time on a landing page takes away from the other elements of a business, with much higher leverage steps that can be taken. I have to learn to accept that tradeoff I’m making.

​Acceptance isn’t easy. My mind grows very comfortable with certain illusions, and when they break, it’s painful. That’s always going to be true, but it in no way makes it less important to accept this (one interesting way to practice accepting scary truths is to read something like this). Be gentle with yourself, and remind yourself what is on the other side of acceptance: deep peace.

Forced Acceptance

When we are avoiding something, there is often a deep fear and anxiety surrounding the avoided “thing”. The more we fear it and push any thoughts away, the worse the thing becomes in our mind: my brain goes, “We seem to be really scared of this thing, so it must be really scary.” Then we avoid it even more. It’s a positive feedback loop that continues until we break ourselves out of it (and that doesn’t always happen).

The break often happens from some external event that stresses the avoided “thing” to the point of forced acceptance. That’s what happened to me; I was living in a lala-land in which I had unlimited time. Then I was forced to accept that I do not, I am severely limited, and must choose what is important.

​So from there, we assume what is on the other end is horrible, right?

Post-Acceptance

On the other end of acceptance is something beautiful, and counterintuitively so. Every time I have spent countless days, weeks, months, or even years avoiding something, I have subconsciously expected something horrible to happen when I recognize the reality of the situation (which is probably why I continued to avoid it). That is almost never the case.

​Post-acceptance leaves us somewhere that is real. Somewhere where footing is solid. Somewhere peaceful.

This is where the Stoics found themselves. Acceptance of death seems intense and scary for someone who hasn’t accepted it (*cough cough* me), but from within it becomes a deeply peaceful experience of understanding and acceptance.

That’s how I have felt with being forced to accept my limited time. At first, it was painful. I realized how much time I have wasted not prioritizing what is really important. I realized how little time I really have. Then, action. I felt capable, like I knew where I was and how to move forward. And from within that, peace in a place I haven’t felt it before.

articles.title: Pseudo-Rewards
articles.subtitle: "I deserve this" isn't going to cut it anymore. Here's what will.
articles.description: "I deserve this" isn't going to cut it anymore. Here's what will.
articles.content:
I held myself to a fairly strict standard throughout June. I ate no junk food. I walked 10k steps every day. I ran 4 days a week, and lifted weights the other 3. I read for 30 minutes every day.

I’m awesome, right?

Well, not so fast. Yesterday I ate a whole pizza. Not like a personal pizza. A multiple-person, large pizza. I mean, I made it through the month, right? Aren’t I supposed to reward myself?

Rewards

Before digging into my pizza mania, I want to address a certain line of thinking I’ve noticed in one of the newer therapeutic flavors of personal development that seems to denounce the idea of earned rewards. The dialogue goes something like this:

“Why are you rewarding hard work?”

“Does that mean you don’t deserve a reward if you don’t do something hard first?”

“What do you believe about yourself that means you don’t deserve good things inherently?”

Everything, then, has to stem from feelings of insufficiency and shame. What if, however, I simply want to train my animal brain to enjoy doing things that are hard for me to do? Does it have to come back to how I feel about myself and the events of my early childhood?

Now we have that out of the way. I am not throwing away the concept of rewards as a whole, because it seems they can be very helpful. But it needs some adjustment.

Pizza Pizza

So I eat this whole pizza. In my head, leading up to it, there are a few thoughts going through my head:

  1. There aren’t any rules about junk food, so I’m totally good to go on this one.

  2. This is not going to feel good.

  3. This is a reward, right? Totally fine to feel shitty after. I’m rewarding myself.

Here’s the most interesting piece. This ordering was the order that my brain put them in. The real conflict was between 1) & 2). 3) was just the tiebreaker brought in to make me feel better about leaning toward 1).

I made a point to not throw away the entire idea of a reward–but this was no reward. This was something dark, a desire to let go of structure and sink back into something comfortable, masquerading as a reward.

Pseudo-Rewards

This seems to be the prevailing mistake that most people make when thinking about rewards. You’ve probably heard it before (maybe even from yourself):

“I’ve been good; I deserve this cookie.”

“I got up early today, so I bought myself lunch.”

“I’ve worked out every day; I deserve a rest.”

These are not rewards. These are back-rationalized decisions. I wanted a cookie, and then the only way I could rationalize eating it was naming all of the ways I’ve been “good”. I really want to go out to lunch, and then I remembered that I got up early, and hence deserve a reward. I’m tired and don’t want to work out, and remembering that I’ve worked out a lot made me feel good enough to take a rest day.

This is where I agree with the therapeutic self-helpers. If you’re doing the thing simply because you want to, tricking yourself into believing it was for some other reason doesn’t help you. Just have it if you’re going to have it. No smoke and mirrors needed.

But. As I said–these are not rewards. These are independent decisions, with their own agendas, masquerading as rewards.

Bonus: Creating Real Rewards

So let’s try. Let’s actually find out how rewards can work for us. We know from countless studies that mammals will exhibit strange behaviors when they are rewarded in certain ways (do your own study and visit a casino). That doesn’t seem to be the case in my situation; I don’t feel any more desire to go do another disciplined monthlong challenge than before I ate that pizza.

Rewards work best when they are:

  1. Not the main motivator. We want the reward to work as a hint for your brain that says hey, strengthen that neural connection; it led me to something good. Find your own motivation for doing the thing, and let the reward be the cherry on top that greases the neural pathways.

  2. Random. This is the one that drives us crazy. Giving random rewards really solidifies the behavior.

  3. Repeated. Make the rewards small enough that your brain can learn to desire the small behaviors that lead to those rewards. Giving yourself one reward at the end of a month of hard work creates a hard problem for your brain to solve: “Wait, which piece got us this thing?”

Here’s an example of a fairly complex reward system I’m experimenting with. It hits the 3 requirements, but may be more complicated than necessary for you.

If you are sold on the idea and want to try something simpler, pick 3 rewards of varying degrees–mobile game, scrolling, a “cheat” snack, etc. Choose a behavior that you want to reinforce (make it significantly large / small to fit the reward size). Make sure you have a real reason to want to reinforce it. Anytime you complete it, roll a die and let that decide your reward–something like 1 or 2 for a small reward, 3 or 4 for nothing, 5 for a medium, and 6 for a large.

Have fun.

articles.title: Running Away From Stress
articles.subtitle: Rumination's fundamental message that I'm missing.
articles.description: Rumination's fundamental message that I'm missing.
articles.content:
“I’m feeling stressed.” I think to myself.

“No, you’re not.” My future self retorts, unheard because of the limits of space-time.

It’s true. I wasn’t feeling stressed. Stress was coming for me, but I was doing everything in my power to run away and throw whatever I could (planning, busyness, rationalization) in its way.

It would have been more truthful if I had instead thought:

“I’m not feeling stressed, but I should be.”

Last night I was lying in bed, ruminating. There were a number of key concerns that kept popping into my mind: many related to business, a tenant, and other random to-dos that I really didn’t want to forget.

Each time something new popped up, I would feel a slight twinge of panic that would quickly get shut down with some good old-fashioned planning.

“I don’t need to feel that, and here’s the logic to support why not.”

Finally, something pushed me over the edge. I couldn’t run from it any longer, and I felt the full rush of stress, panic, anxiety, whatever you want to call it. And then, I went right to sleep, finally at peace.

It is my inclination that the ‘problem’ of rumination is not solved by thinking more. It’s not because I worry too much. It seems to be the opposite: I don’t worry enough (and by worry, I mean accepting and not pushing away the emotion we’re talking about).

Rumination isn’t a problem of the thinking mind. It is a repeated attempt to use my thinking mind to solve a problem that has nothing to do with it. The ‘fix’ isn’t to stop thinking. The ‘fix’ is to confront the problem where it lies.

In my example, it seemed as if my body simply wanted me to feel this certain emotion. The more and more I pushed it away, thinking “oh, I’m stressed, this sucks,” the more my emotional brain went “Just feel it one fucking time, and then you won’t be!”

Take a second to imagine the hopeless frustration of an entity incapable of communicating but through emotion, whose one job is to relay a message to a separate entity who is completely disinterested in listening to emotion.

It’s like having a deaf child and refusing to learn ASL, all while failing to even recognize that they are not capable of using the type of communication we are familiar with.

So that’s where I was, my emotional brain getting more and more frustrated and my rational brain failing to see the sole message it was trying to get through to me. It wasn’t until my rational brain was overwhelmed that the message got through, which begs the question:

What if I had listened earlier?

articles.title: Willpower Assets
articles.subtitle: Wont and Wellbeing
articles.description: Wont and Wellbeing
articles.content:
Most days lately, I’ve been running out of steam around midday. My energy (and motivation) comes in hot after my first cup of coffee. From there, it’s an uphill battle to get back. It’s not just energy either; it’s attitude. On days when I feel drained, I also feel less capable, less ready to take on the world and any of its problems that dare face me.

When I think about willpower (my overall ability to do what I set out to do), there are two easy pieces that I think get overlooked. The first is physical well-being; the second is behavioral wont.

At a given moment, I may feel as though I “can’t do it” and need a rest. Or I may feel like I’m on top of the world, ready to blast through the next wall I see. In the prior situation, it feels impossible to do the simplest things: even sitting at my computer and checking my to-do list. In the latter, it feels easy and enjoyable.​

Most of us associate “willpower” with the first (and that’s the kind of willpower I’ve been trying to exert recently). What if a more effective strategy was not to fight through the type of momentary impedance as the initial scenario placed in front of us, but instead to focus on changing to the second state?

Rather than “How can I get through this?” the question becomes “How can this be easy?” or “How can I enjoy this?” This puts us in a different frame, arguably a better one with a longer time horizon. Fighting it, in the best case, results in a momentary burst of energy. Switching states results in that, plus more.

That’s why I am thinking of the elements of my “state” as an asset, a regularly paying off feature of where I’m at in life. Fighting through low energy is like working a manual labor job; improving my state to make it easier is like buying a machine to handle the work for me. It’s an investment, but it pays off the more I get to use it.

Willpower assets come in 2 forms, as I mentioned above: behavioral wont and physical well-being. These are the 2 ways we make decision-making easier. Having either one pays off over the duration that it is maintained.

Behavioral Wont

Behavioral wont is the set of things we are used to, or what feels normal and expected. If I think that running is a crazy activity and I rarely see anyone else do it, I won’t naturally think it’s a good decision to do it. Monkey see monkey more-likely-to do.

When people get into running, they’re far more likely to get into it if they join a run club. They see others doing it, and it becomes extremely normal to run. That tips the scales heavily in their decision-making process.

It isn’t just other people; it’s also about what we make normal. If you are comfortable writing every day, because it’s something you’ve done for years, the decision to write will happen quickly and without thought. For someone who wants to write but never has, writing is not contained in their wont, and they will likely struggle.

Behavioral wont is built over time. The mistake many of us make is expecting that our brain’s understanding of what is normal can shift instantaneously simply because we want it to. It doesn’t work this way. Updating behavioral wont is a very doable process, but it requires time for the brain to reset to the new normal. Transitioning slowly and consistently is the upfront cost that will pay off handsomely once you are the owner of this type of asset.​

Physical Wellbeing

If behavioral wont tips the scales naturally, physical wellbeing puts my hand on the scale.

Do you ever notice how your eating patterns change when you haven’t slept well? I’ve noticed it myself. I crave food differently when my body is not in its 100% state.

When I don’t workout, I’m typically in a worse mood, and less likely to do something about it. If I eat poorly, I have less energy.

All of these things tie into this idea: We are able to make the best long-term decisions when our momentary health is optimized. This is an asset that pays off immediately. You can sleep well one night and upon waking have about twice the energy that you felt the day before. Go for one run and notice the motivation that you’ll be able to ride for hours after.

Neither of these involves “grit”. Rather, they both make grit feel less, well, “gritty”. When building willpower (the ability to take actions that reflect your values), having some assets that make it easier isn’t such a bad idea.

articles.title: Natural Drives and "Why"'s
articles.subtitle: When pushing past our limits becomes shockingly easy
articles.description: When pushing past our limits becomes shockingly easy
articles.content:
A few days ago, I went for a run with my dog, Reba.

We made it to our halfway point, which meant it was time to turn around. She decided that instead of running back, she was going to sit in place and simply endure the light tugging on her leash and coercing I sent her way.

She’s 50% Siberian Husky. We were in the Texas sun. This was not what she was built for.

As much as I wanted to feel for her and “see her struggle”, I knew we needed to get home. And we were a few miles from there. So I dropped the leash and started running back without her.

I figured “She’ll catch up, and she can run at her own pace.”

We were on a trail that doesn’t cross any roads, so I felt ok about her being off-leash. Plus, she was so tired, there was no way she’d run off. Right?

So we ran like that for some time. She was about 20 paces behind me, and every minute I’d check on her. We stopped off for a dip and drink from the creek, then continued.

When we were about a quarter mile from home, I saw a switch flip in her brain.

Here she was lolly-gagging along, tongue hanging out of the side of her mouth, when something moved in the woods to our left.

Her ears shot up, and her entire demeanor changed in a heartbeat. The dog I had failed to convince to run with me sprinted past me and veered off into the woods, where I saw a fully grown white-tailed deer looking out at us.

My point in telling you this is not to say that you should look for deer if your dog is tired. In fact, quite the opposite, and I learned my lesson with this one.

​

What I can say is that the energy and willingness to exert it changed so drastically in my dog that I almost couldn’t believe it. As she sprinted after that deer, I saw zero hesitation, zero fatigue, not even a second thought about whether her body had the energy.

​And on top of that, she looked like she was having the time of her life.

When I hear things about “pushing past your limits”, I’m often quickly turned off. I imagine a grueling process of pain and discomfort.

This story shows a different option. With the proper fuel (and in my dogs case, one of the most potent and deeply rooted sources of fuel) we are capable of not only pushing ourselves to new places, but also doing it in a way that feels exciting, fun, and natural.

That’s what understanding your “why” is really about. It’s not about forcing a lifestyle upon yourself or trying to create masochism for harder workouts.

It’s finding the things you care about, the things that give you energy naturally, and allowing those to fuel you in the direction you really want to go.

articles.title: Negotiating
articles.subtitle: And why it's not always a bad thing
articles.description: And why it's not always a bad thing
articles.content:
This week I had a really cool guest on the podcast, a man named Chris Harris.

There were a number of shocking and inspiring stories he told me from his life: watching his mom get arrested, being homeless as a teenager, having brain surgery (literally 8 weeks before we recorded this episode), and a number of other crazy occurrences.

Yet, with all of those extremely unique experiences he shared, one seemingly inconsequential thing he said has been sticking with me:

“I don’t negotiate with myself.”

This morning, I woke up at 7:30am with an alarm. I was having a good dream (I don’t remember what it was about, but I remember feeling relaxed and excited) when my vibrating watch shook me back to reality.

I knew I was behind on sleep from the day before (early-morning flights will do that), but I had also set out my running clothes and shoes the night before, making it very hard for me to ignore. I thanked and cursed my previous self as I tried to decide what to do.

I was negotiating.

I couldn’t just go back to sleep. That didn’t seem right to just throw out the plan completely. But man, I was not quite ready to go run. So I came to an agreement with myself: I would put on my running clothes, and then on my way out I could sleep on the couch for 30 minutes, if I decided at that point that I still wanted to.

​I got my shorts and running shoes on, and walked out to take my promised nap…

To find Reba (my dog) sitting smack dab in the center of the couch. She looked up at me as if to say: Good luck getting me up, I didn’t make any plans to run this morning.​

I ended up taking a short nap on the chair next to her, and though it took some convincing for her, we ended up doing the run 30 minutes late, at 8 am.

I’m now writing this an hour later, and I feel pretty good about that. Would I have been better off if I said “No negotiating” and went right out at 7:30? It’s quite possible. The Chris Harris method may be the optimal one.​

It also may not be what most of us need to hear.

I want us to imagine now that there are two parts of each of us. It’s a simplification that, I think, works here.

One part wants comfort. It wants to relax, it wants to feel good right now.

The other part wants to achieve. It wants to make progress, and it wants to move forward.

For a lot of people, these two parts are in constant tension. Then, there are those who “don’t negotiate”. In other words, one of these parts has taken control, and there is no longer a dialogue between them when it comes to decision making.

In Chris’ case, that seems to be a good thing. He goes to the gym without a second thought (even after brain surgery, which stopped him from actually working out, he still went to the gym). He doesn’t negotiate.

For every case like his, there are a thousand people who also don’t negotiate. Those are the people in whom the comfort part has begun to make the calls. They could say the exact same thing that he does: “I don’t negotiate. I don’t even consider going to the gym.”

The problem isn’t negotiating. The problem is not giving power to the part that we want to be better at negotiating.

articles.title: Success
articles.subtitle: Happiness is just a decision (and some time) away
articles.description: Happiness is just a decision (and some time) away
articles.content:
I often hear podcast interviews in which someone prefaces a story about themselves with something like, “Some people would see my life as successful.” Sometimes it’s more tongue-in-cheek, when a very accomplished person says something like “I’ve done a few things that weren’t completely stupid”.

It is a completely understandable display of humility, but beneath it lies something more interesting. It seems almost as if they are saying “I’ve done the things that make me successful, but I don’t really know whether I actually am successful”.

In this humble brag, they’re actually revealing that there may be confusion about what they have done. And that’s why today, I want to talk about success.

Ten Months

I have spent 10 months working on something that has netted me $0. In fact, it has netted me less if you count the money I have put into it, and much less if you count the time.

For some reason, it still feels like just a few. When I realize how long it has been, I feel it. I feel like I’ve made a mistake, like I’ve been unsuccessful. After all, what is success but a monetary value?

Then I return to reality. I recognize the truth of the situation. I have spent ten months of my life working on a project that I want to be working on, that I literally built from scratch.

In this frame, the $0 income is more of an inconvenience than a dealbreaker. I should probably figure that part out, but it sure as hell doesn’t mean I haven’t been successful.​

Defining success

Rather than going in this roundabout way where it takes 10 months to define what success means–my claim today is that deciding what success means when beginning a pursuit is a way to get much more fulfillment out of the act of pursuing. It protects against future ‘oh shit it’s been 10 months’ moments, because it maintains awareness throughout.

Consider what you are spending your time on. Pick something that is taking significant time (or that you wish to begin spending more time on), and do two things:​

  1. Determine how most people would measure your success in this pursuit. If you are wanting to go to the gym more, the external measure may be how impressed your coworkers are as your body adapts.

  2. Determine how you would like to define success. You might want to feel healthier, to have more energy, or be more athletic. You might even just want to impress your coworkers.

Importantly, these can be the same thing. I am not telling you not to use external motivators or not to listen to the outside world. However, I am saying that listening to the external world is a choice, and it’s yours (and mine) to make.

​There are still constraints in this world. Money is a necessary component of survival, as is health. You have to respect those as pieces of reality. But when it comes to deciding what it is that I am optimizing for, what it would mean for me to be successful, that is completely up to me.

articles.title: Breaking Cycles
articles.subtitle: Where biology and physiology play bigger roles than I've realized
articles.description: Where biology and physiology play bigger roles than I've realized
articles.content:
Cycles are a common theme in behavior and well-being. We’ve discussed positive and negative feedback loops and how each of those can create behavior cycles. Specifically sticky are the positive ones, that ramp up (or down) until we are really stuck in a behavior.

The feedback loop I’ve found myself in lately is one of poor sleep. Not sleeping too little, but getting poor quality sleep. That happens for a multitude of reasons, but I think I have picked out the biggest one, and it’s perfect for this topic: mistimed sleep due to caffeine consumption.

In other words, my sleep time has been getting pushed back, which leads to less-than-ideal sleep, which leads to more desire for caffeine, which leads to my sleep time getting pushed back, and on and on.

Today, I’m going to explore ideas around breaking this cycle that I am likely to follow and with extrapolation potential (I could just say “quit caffeine tomorrow and go to bed at 10pm”, but that wouldn’t be that helpful to anyone else).

Bedtime

There is clear data, by now, showing that timing of sleep matters for health, on the same level of importance as duration of sleep. It has been shown that large variations in bedtime correlate with higher BMI, fat mass, and insulin resistance. Three things that, generally speaking, correspond to poor health and feeling less than optimal.​

This problem, then, is of utmost importance. Every day that I am not asleep by the same time as the night before is building on this problem–and making me more likely to continue building on it in future days.

Why patterns exists

I am tempted first to look into why these cycles even happen in the first place, and to see if there’s any way that the cycle can be cleanly broken without too much difficulty.​

With negative cycles (not to be confused with negative feedback, as these are positive feedback loops we are discussing), I am often being pushed into a reactive state. Not only is that happening, it is the primary reason I end up in the cycle. Rather than making decisions, I am reacting to what is happening.​

For example, I may decide today to stop drinking so much caffeine. Tomorrow, however, if I wake up a tired wretch, I may just say forget it and run to the coffee machine. I am reacting immediately to the circumstances, in an attempt to feel better.

So two things are happening.

  1. I want to feel better.

  2. I am in a reactive state.

These two work in tandem to provide a foundation for disaster. Wanting to feel better is not a bad or unnatural state in the slightest: it only becomes a problem when all other considerations are thrown away at the behest of my next gratification.

In other words, reaction places too much emphasis on fixing the current problem at hand.

Breaking the cycle

So we have a bit more understanding now. First, that sleep regularity is actually really important to be healthy and happy (and to continue sleeping regularly). Second, being in a reactive state keeps us in cycles.

I want to offer one of the simplest and (maybe) most interesting ideas I’ve stumbled upon recently. It’s based in commonly known practices, but the understanding is based on a connection that I had never recognized before now.​

The magic answer is… taking a few deep breaths.

Ok, ok. That’s not an exciting answer, nor does it feel worthy of your time to have read to this point. Hang in there.

Biology and Me

The connection I’ve been seeing more and more is between my subjective state and my physiological state. It also comes with a breakdown of what we commonly think of as the “self”.

Recently, I was in a group and noticed myself overthinking what I was saying or about to say, which led me to withhold my social contributions. By many definitions, it was social anxiety.

In the state of shut down, I remembered a recent conversation in which a friend of mine had brought to my attention the idea of “fight-or-flight”, and how many of us live our lives in this (reactive) state. On a whim (and because I wasn’t doing anything else, sitting there silently), I tried taking a few deep breaths, really focusing on relaxing. As if my magic, the thoughts and emotions that were holding me back simply stopped popping up, and I was able to rejoin naturally and without fear.​

The profound part of this all is the way in which these thoughts and feelings went away. I think many of us assume that overcoming something will require a fight in which we defeat the debilitating thoughts one by one. Stepping out of this is recognizing that there is no “defeating” these thoughts, at least not in the way we think. These thoughts don’t live by the laws of logic; they can’t be debated. It is in recognizing that they are coming from a source that has been shaken so dramatically that it is spewing fearful and (often) incorrect ideas because it is trying to understand why it feels this level of danger. The correct response is to bring the system back to a place of safety, rather than fight the thoughts and emotions.​

An animal that is in danger will highly prioritize an action that brings relief as soon as possible. It makes sense to do that. The problem is that 99% of the time, I am not facing real danger. My biology is misdiagnosing my surroundings.

Bringing it in

The way to break a cycle is to bring oneself out of a reactive state. The way to move out of a reactive state is to restore the body to a state of relaxation and safety.

Let’s walk through this with my first example.​

  1. I go to sleep late, because I’m not that tired when I usually go to bed.

  2. I wake up, and I don’t feel great. I recognize that coffee will make me feel slightly better, right now. I don’t (yet) consider whether it will continue this negative cycle.

  3. I stop myself for a second. I recognize that I am in a reactive state, which makes short-term rewards seem extremely valuable. I take a second to breathe and notice, and I begin to feel less “on edge”.

  4. I magically begin to see the decision to have coffee differently–not because I consciously made myself think any specific way, but because I have set up my biological system to place less emphasis on feeling better, right now.

  5. I decide whether to have a coffee.

articles.title: Remembering How Things Can Be
articles.subtitle: When it comes, listen
articles.description: When it comes, listen
articles.content:
I’ve been sleeping poorly, eating poorly, and missing exercise. There are reasons I need not go into (not to excuse it or to say that those things weren’t possible for me), but I’ve noticed a drawback in my day-to-day experience as a result.

That comes in the form of less energy, less excitement, and a higher reliance on instant gratification - coffee, food, checking my phone, working distractedly on numerous projects at any one time. Along with that comes a general feeling that things are dull and boring, and will stay that way.

Growing up, I remember feeling this way at times. There’s a certain fear and helplessness that becomes associated with feeling “bad” because of the inability to see beyond it. When I felt anxious, low energy (depressed), or fearful, it seemed inevitable and eternal. That was simply the way it would be: this is how I feel now, forever.

The worst part isn’t the feeling. The worst part is the mental chatter telling me that this is my fault, and that this dull and reliant existence is the way I will be from here on out.

Remembering how things can be

As an adult, I’ve noticed that the fundamental experience I’ve described hasn’t changed. There are still the same stories, the same feelings, and the same impulses.

However, there’s something else, something that is rare and as exciting and beautiful as it is rare. It’s a thought, a reminder, that visits quietly and briefly. It whispers in my ear, “Remember how things have been.” That’s it.

That quiet reminder gives me a chance. It’s an opportunity to see the larger picture that has been obfuscated by the particular fear or apathy that has taken over. It’s not the end, but it could be the beginning.

Listening

As I mentioned, it’s often very quiet and brief. I’ve had the experience of having this blinding beam of optimism in the midst of an episode of stimulation-reliant living, and after not acting on the recognition immediately, I quickly forgot and returned to my ways.

Then there are times when I did act on it, and I built upon the optimism that had been spontaneously generated. That feeling rarely comes on its own, and like a seed, it must be nourished and protected to continue to exist. Listen closely, and take these as the gift they are.

articles.title: The Depth of Sadness
articles.subtitle: A rough take on a challenging emotion, written at 30,000 feet
articles.description: A rough take on a challenging emotion, written at 30,000 feet
articles.content:
Sadness is an emotion I’ve never felt comfortable with, much less accustomed to. It always felt like a fight—either it was something I shouldn’t feel, or at the very least, something I did not want to feel.

Yet it comes, the unstoppable force that forces the yielding of my “immovable” stubbornness to feel it. Sadness is an inevitability of life. It’s scary and uncomfortable. At the same time, there is something comforting about falling into its embrace and feeling into the richness that it brings to experience.

For me, sadness hits like a hole in my lower chest. If I let myself lean into it, it almost feels like I’m falling through my chest into my abdominal space. It’s deep, viscerally deep.

Sometimes when some happening brings upon the sadness, as is the case today, I notice that the feeling in my chest and stomach is not new, like a sore my tongue has just discovered and won’t stop probing. The feeling has been there, and this difficult event has led me to finally explore it.

There’s somewhere to exist peacefully in there. It’s actually not scary, and it’s actually not uncomfortable. Those are only resistances, like my body’s last line of defense before feeling something real. There’s nothing to avoid. It’s an ultimate way to honor life, that we experience the very depth of sadness that loving can cause.

articles.title: The Novelty Drive-Thru
articles.subtitle: "Junk" stimulation's missing component
articles.description: "Junk" stimulation's missing component
articles.content:
My brain is a stimulation-seeking device. It is built to explore, to find the most interesting inputs it can. This is a good thing.

This is the reason that anything gets done. I wouldn’t go back to Jiu Jitsu if I wasn’t hoping to learn something, or complete a submission, or meet someone interesting enough to make it worth it. I wouldn’t write this every week if I didn’t think there was a chance that I would find some new insight that would be profound and exciting to discover.

Our exploration for novelty is a good instinct. However, for most of us, it has been hijacked.

Pathologization

The issue that most of us face with stimulation is akin to the dilemma of processed food. We all have a desire to eat food that works with our bodies’ systems to tell us when we need nourishment. That desire is good, but it isn’t perfect. It can be captured, and has been for many of us. Engineered foods hit our systems in a way that confuses them and makes them believe that it is nourishing in a way that it is not, leading to overeating and malnourishment.

So what’s the solution? To stop eating altogether?

Of course not. We all know this.​

This is the problem we run into with stimulation. We have hundreds of unhealthy sources of stimulation hitting us every single day. The solution, though, is not to denounce stimulation and novelty. This is not a call to join an ashram and spend your days meditating.

Rather, sticking with the food analogy, the guidance follows that we should seek out “healthy” sources of stimulation.

Spotting Unhealthy Stimulation

If you eat a lot of fruit, you will likely not become unhealthier because of it. However, if you flip that and drink a lot of fruit juice, over time, you may find yourself facing increased inflammation, diabetes, or even heart disease. This is not intuitive–it seems that if the fruit is healthy, each of its component parts should be as well. The problem, as we have collectively learned, is that our bodies do not respond the same to each piece in isolation. It’s not about what we are consuming when we drink fruit juice. It’s what we are not.

This sets us up perfectly to understand unhealthy stimulation. It is missing something some key component of healthy stimulation.

Let’s say one day I go out to an event. I’m nervous to go, but I end up meeting a number of cool people. I connect with a few with the intention to keep in contact. It’s exciting. Another day I pull up Instagram and scroll through 20 videos in the span of a few minutes. I feel excited during this as well.

After the event, I feel fulfilled and accomplished. After scrolling IG, I feel… empty.

What was the difference? Both seemed to start with excitement, and then completely diverged from each other. My brain was just doing it’s job of seeking excitement, and in one case was rewarded, in the other heavily penalized. How can it make sense of this?​

The key component that was missed in scenario #2 was what happened at the start of scenario #1: I had to work for the excitement–there was a lead-up, I had to exert energy to get there, and initiate conversation. I had to go through something challenging (nervousness) in order to get the reward. It seems that some type of energy expenditure is a key component of healthy stimulation.

Responsibility

Unfortunately, our brains, for the most part, struggle to understand the unhealthiness of unhealthy stimulation. They’ve come to understand sugar as the “good” part of fruit, and similarly see the dopamine spike as the “good” part of an experience. Because of that, they do not discern between the ones that require work–in fact, they will more likely avoid those (why more people are addicted to social media than to working out).

The onus is on us. I can’t depend on my brain to make the decision, and so I must make it. I don’t keep processed junk food around the house, nor should I keep processed junk stimulation.

What I can’t do is get rid of it completely: I will always be able to access it with a few clicks or taps (the McDonald’s drive-thru of the digital world). But I can control how much it is allowed to infiltrate my life. I can choose the apps on my phone. I can choose which can notify me. I can choose which companies are allowed to email me. I can build routines around how I use the internet. I choose which junk is allowed in my house.

articles.title: Choosing Where You Want To Be
articles.subtitle: What piano can teach us about life and learning
articles.description: What piano can teach us about life and learning
articles.content:
I wish I could tell you how to turn your life into the exact life you want, tomorrow. I wish I could do that for myself, today. I can’t, but I do have some thoughts on the subject.

​Learning something new

I’ve been working on a challenging piano piece (for my ability level) for 6+ months now. Almost every day, I spend a little bit of time practicing the parts that I have already learned and slowly adding on to what I can “get through”–if I’m lucky, I’ll be able to play through one measure (a section of a music piece that in this case represents 4 “beats”) that I couldn’t the day before.

Most measures take me a few days to get the hang of enough to play them directly from the previous measure. The progress is painstakingly slow. I have to fight and claw for each measure, which, when all is said and done, amounts to ~2 seconds of playing time in the final piece. Yet, I find it worth it, and I continue to do it.

Now, I’d like to find what lessons I can take from this extremely slow process that I have followed steadfastly and hopefully apply elsewhere in my life.

The key components

There are a few things that seem to be keeping me going on this piano piece. Those seem to be:

  • The end goal. If there wasn’t something I was working towards (being able to play through an entire piece that I find great), I would never have had the motivation to get started, much less continue at it for this long.
